Jash Shah
TY BTech, Computer Engineering, 2024.
DE SHAW | Interview Experience
DE Shaw India (DESIS) was the first company to visit our campus for internships for 3rd Year Students
Eligibility Criteria : A total of 176 students were eligible
For CS/IT Students, CGPA criteria was 7+
For Circuital Students, CGPA criteria was 8+
Online Assessment
1st August, 2022
The proctored online assessment was conducted on the Hackerrank platform. Total time allotted was 90
minutes. There were 3 coding questions and each of them had an individual time limit of 25, 35 & 35
minutes respectively. It was not permitted to navigate between the questions - we can move to the next
question if we either submit it or the question's time limit gets exhausted.
1. Similar Strings - 25 Minutes Time limit
You've been given 2 strings a and b. You have to determine whether those 2 strings are similar or not.
The criteria for similarity of 2 strings was:
1.
If the 2 strings are equal, they are similar
2.
If the 2 strings are unequal and either of them (or both) is of odd length, they cannot be similar.
3.
If the 2 strings are unequal and both of even lengths, then we can split them to check for
similarity if either of the conditions satisfy:
a.
First half of a is similar to the second half of b AND the second half of a is similar to the
first half of b.

b. First half of a is similar to the first half of b AND the second half of a is similar to the
second half of b.
Consider the following testcase:
"ab" and "ba" are the 2 strings - since these are of even lengths and they are unequal, we can observe
that the first half of the first string (i.e., "a") and the second half of the second string (i.e., "a") match.
Similarly, the second half of the first string and first half of the second string match too. Hence, these 2
strings can be deemed similar.
The solution I implemented is similar to the one mentioned here:
https://www.geeksforgeeks.org/check-whether-two-strings-are-equivalent-or-not-according-to-given-condi
tion/
This was a fairly straight forward question and I was able to solve it in approx 20 mins.
2. Subarray Deletion - 35 minutes time limit
You've been given an array of positive integers. You're asked to find the number of subarrays such that
removing that subarray results in an array (which must not be empty) that is sorted in a strictly
increasing order.
Consider the following testcase:
Let the array be a = [1, 3, 2]
If we remove the subarray [2], then we get the resultant array as [1, 3] which is a sorted array. Similarly,
removing the subarray [3] results into the array [1, 2] which is sorted.
My solution was using a sliding window approach.
https://www.geeksforgeeks.org/length-of-smallest-subarray-to-be-removed-such-that-the-remaining-array-
is-sorted/amp/
This was solved fairly quickly too, again within approx 20 mins.
3. Classical 0/1 Knapsack - 35 minutes time limit
It was literally just a generic knapsack problem without any variation.
This took some time since I kinda messed up the memoization tables in the beginning, but solved it
eventually.

Most of my time was spent on covering all test cases. I could find the initial approach fairly
quickly(usually the first guess), but improving the solution to fit all test cases is where you’ve to go
back and reassess that first approach and optimize it as much as possible.
The results of the online assessment were released after 5 days on 6th August, 2022. A total of 17
students were shortlisted for the interviews.
Technical Round 1
8th August, 2022
This round was conducted on Hackerrank Codepair. It has several facilities - an
interactive IDE, whiteboard, chat window and voice/video room.
Before starting with any DSA question, they asked me questions about my previous projects. They were
quite impressed with the quantity of projects on my resume at the time. They asked me a few questions
on an ML backend I had set up on one of my hackathon projects, where we had won(fyi Sarvagnya (the
other candidate selected for DE. Shaw was my teammate)). But around 30 mins of my Round 1 was spent
discussing my Google Summer of Code, 2022 project. They asked me pretty detailed questions, but I
was very comfortable with this, so having that project on my resume turned out to be a big plus!!
I wasn’t asked any questions on OS, DBMS, or any other core subjects but a lot of other candidates were.
I coded all my DSA problems in Python 3.
PS: They did ask me(in both rounds) the reason for this choice, and I just mentioned that I’m more
comfortable with and quicker in Python. I offered to switch to C or C++ if they wished, but they were fins
with Python.
Question 1 - 20/25 mins
https://www.geeksforgeeks.org/roots-tree-gives-minimum-height/
I struggled a bit on this one initially, but kept on talking throughout and the interviewer guided me along.
Eventually I was able to give a good enough solution.
I wasn’t asked to code this question.
PS: Never forget to calculate the time complexity of each problem. Don’t consider time complexity as a
separate question, it is part of the solution.
Question 2 - 15/20 mins

https://leetcode.com/problems/number-of-atoms/
The solution was pretty straightforward to grasp for me. I mentioned a good enough solution quickly
enough and the interviewer then asked me to code it. I wasn’t able to finish the whole thing before the
deadline, but managed to code about 85% of it. There was some syntax error due to which I couldn’t run
the code, but the interviewer didn’t mind it.
PS: Since I didn’t know about the existence of the whiteboard feature, I described the entire problem in
the comments of the code and also gave NumPy formatted docstrings for my functions as I wrote them.
Out of the 17 students interviewed for Round 1, 5 students were shortlisted for
Round 2. I was luckily one of them.
Technical Round 2
8th August, 2022
I was firstly greeted by the two interviewers and they were very friendly. Both of them introduced
themselves first and then asked me to introduce myself. Then they asked me some questions on my
resume and the projects/tech-stack I'd worked on. Again, a bunch of questions on my GSoC project.
I was asked only one question with its implementation.
Question 1 - 45+ mins
You are given 2 strings. And you’ve to find the longest common subsequence. But here’s the catch: given
an integer k, each character in the second string can be increased or decreased ci times, such that
sum(ci) over all i is less than k, to get the LCS.
Eg:
String 1:  a x d a j
String 2: a c b y l
And k = 6,
So my second string will be changed as follows:
a
c

b -> c -> d  (c2 = 2), moving ahead by two alphabets
y -> z -> a (c4 = 2), ‘z’ can move to ‘a’ and ‘a’ can move back to ‘a’
l -> k -> j   (c5 = 2), moving behind my two alphabets
String 2 becomes: a c d a j
d a j is the LCS
This is a problem I(or anyone of the other candidates I asked later) had never seen before. The only
saving grace was that at its core it was still LCS. So, I started by describing the DP approach to LCS and
how the tabulation for the same will be done. And as I kept talking, I realized that we can use recursion
for each cell in the table. At each char where we have a choice to increase or decrease it, we make two
recursive calls, where each call will lead to a different table and choose the one which leads to the max
LCS.
Further, I mentioned we can use memoization to eliminate the tables which were already generated. I
even mentioned more fine grained tabulation for each cell in each table. If it had already been calculated
for a previous tabulation, then using appropriate data structure, we can use those values from memory.
Honestly speaking, I have no idea how I managed to come up with such a good solution in the first go.
But the interviewer was quite impressed, and asked me to immediately start coding it midway through my
explanation. I used multidim lists for all the data structures and while the code was quite convoluted in its
first draft, I managed to make it quite clean, presentable and working by the end
Follow Up
Since my coding question ran upwards of 45 mins, I was relieved to realize that I wasn’t going to be asked
any further coding questions. The second interviewer then asked me a few basic questions on OS and C,
which I managed to answer.
At the end of the interview, I was asked if I had any questions for them. Always ask a question, it shows you are
interested. I asked them what the actual work is like in an Internship at D.E. Shaw and what the past experiences
of them as mentors have been like. They happily answered both questions.
The results for this final round came at about 9:40 PM and 2 students were
selected. I was fortunate to be one of them!

Tips
Related to DSA:
I personally had never delved too deep into either Competitive Programming or regularly practicing DSA.
The only resource I relied on were my DSA notes I had made for Computer Engineering Sem 3 while
watching Abdul Bari’s Algorithms Playlist. I would highly recommend referring to Sarvagnya’s experience
for some actually good resources.
Related to Core CS (OS, DBMS, OOPS):
GeeksForGeeks, Gate Smashers, Neso Academy are your best friends for college courses or otherwise.
Try to understand the core concepts instead of mugging up the material. I personally make notes on
GDocs or on a Note making app on my Tab, but a simple notebook and pen to roughly note down
concepts while reading or watching these resources should be more than enough.
Related to Interviews:
1.
Be very cool, calm, collected and confident.
2.
Speak up without hesitation. Be a good communicator and listener. Go on clearing any doubts
you have throughout the interview.
3.
Be friendly and easy to talk to. The more nervous you are, the more serious the mood will be.
There were points where I laughed or acknowledged my own stupidity during the interview and
the interviewers were quite in for it.
4.
The interviewers are the only other humans besides you in that call. And they are there to help
you. Use this to its maximum advantage.
5.
Stay hydrated and isolated during the interview. Take short walks or breaks in between.
Most importantly, this isn’t the end all be all. There are many great companies out there, and many
internships to be had. Take it as it comes!
All the best!
